To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the 14C signatures of mobilized aquatic organic carbon are highly variable in Arctic headwaters, 2) the mobilized aquatic carbon is predominantly modern in age and has a relatively short residence time in the aquatic environment, and 3) mobilized aquatic carbon contains a significant amount of old carbon, but the source of this carbon and the implications for the permaforst carbon feedback remain unclear.

(1) mobilization of pre-industrial organic carbon from Arctic headwaters is widespread; (2) this carbon is mobilized as DOC and CO2 and is likely derived from the active layer; (3) mobilization of old carbon is enhanced during the snow-free season; and (4) the presence of pre-industrial carbon in Arctic headwaters does not necessarily indicate a net PCF.
we found that old carbon is mobilized into headwaters of the Canadian Arctic, which may be indicative of a permafrost carbon feed-back.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mobilization of old carbon into Arctic headwater systems, and the implications for the PCF.
the fate of old carbon in permafrost headwaters.
how mobilized soil organic carbon (SOC) in permafrost headwater streams is aged and how it is transported downstream.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Arctic headwaters of the Mackenzie River are a source of CO2 to the atmosphere, but the magnitude of that source is unknown and requires further study.
the mobilization of old carbon from Arctic headwaters is a natural phenomenon, and that the presence of old carbon does not necessarily indicate a positive PCF.
the Arctic permafrost region is not a source of old carbon at this time, but that it is likely to become one in the future as permafrost thaws and the active layer deepens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

mobilization of soil/surface sediments into headwater systems in the western Canadian Arctic is a significant source of CO2 and DOC to downstream systems, and the majority of this mobilized carbon is of 'old' origin.
the Arctic is not as 'young' as it seems.
the permafrost is a significant source of carbon for Arctic headwaters, and the age of the mobilized carbon is increasing with time, indicating a possible increase in the rate of carbon mobilization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Arctic is not a 'carbon time bomb' waiting to go off.
mobilization of pre-industrial carbon is occurring in permafrost headwaters, and that this mobilization increases as the active layer depth deepens.
the Arctic is a dynamic region, and the PCF is not a static phenomenon.
